title: World Geography · Episode 1
chapters: Everest: the roof of the world

units.t: World Geography. Episode one.
In this episode: The continents, Antarctica: the continent of extremes, Rivers and mountains and Everest: the roof of the world.
Part one. The continents.
Ask how many continents there are and the answer depends on where you went to school.
Even the shape of the world on your wall is a compromise.
A matter of convention.
Continents are not neatly separated by oceans.
Africa joins Asia at the Isthmus of Suez, and North and South America meet at Panama.
The list is an agreed way of dividing land, and traditions differ.
Australian schools teach seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America.
Much of Latin America teaches the Americas as one, making six.
Some geographers join Europe and Asia as Eurasia, because no ocean divides them.
The five Olympic rings stand for the inhabited continents, leaving out Antarctica.
Join Africa to Eurasia as Afro-Eurasia and you have four.
The Europe–Asia line is conventionally drawn along the Urals, the Caucasus and the Bosphorus.
Istanbul straddles it, though geologically Europe sits on the same plate as most of Asia.
The giants and the smallest.
Asia covers about 44 million square kilometres, roughly 30 per cent of Earth's land, and holds about 4.
8 billion people, close to 60 per cent of humanity, 2024.
Africa is second in area, at about 30 million square kilometres, and has the fastest-growing population, about 1.
5 billion, 2024.
Antarctica, at about 14 million square kilometres, is larger than Europe or Australia but has no permanent residents, only a few thousand researchers in summer.
It also has the highest average elevation, because it is covered in ice.
Australia is the smallest continent, at about 7.
7 million square kilometres.
It is also the flattest, with an average elevation of only about 330 metres.
Australia and Zealandia.
The continent of Australia, sometimes called Sahul, is the landmass on the Australian continental shelf: the mainland, Tasmania and New Guinea.
In the last ice age, when sea levels were far lower, dry land joined them and people walked between them.
Oceania is a broader region that adds the Pacific islands of Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia.
New Zealand belongs to Oceania, not the Australian continent.
In 2017, geologists made the case that a mostly submerged landmass to the south-west, Zealandia, Te Riu-a-Māui, is a continent.
It covers about 5 million square kilometres, but roughly 94 per cent lies under the sea.
New Zealand and New Caledonia are its highest parts.
Not every geographer lists it, but many now accept it.
Drifting continents.
The continents are not fixed.
They ride on tectonic plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.
Around 300 million years ago most land was joined in the supercontinent Pangaea, which later broke apart.
Australia was part of its southern half, Gondwana, with Antarctica, Africa, South America and India.
Zealandia broke away from Gondwana from around 85 million years ago.
Australia separated from Antarctica within the last 50 million years or so, and has drifted north ever since, at about 7 centimetres a year.
That adds up: Australia's official coordinate system, GDA2020, was updated to account for that drift, shifting positions by about 1.
8 metres so maps line up with GPS.
Every map distorts.
You cannot flatten a sphere without stretching it, so every world map distorts something.
The familiar Mercator projection, designed in 1569 by the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator for sailors, shows a constant compass bearing as a straight line.
The price is that areas balloon towards the poles.
Greenland looks about as big as Africa, yet Africa is roughly 14 times larger.
Australia looks smaller than it is next to Europe.
Equal-area maps, such as the Gall-Peters projection, show true sizes but squash shapes.
Compromise projections like the Winkel tripel balance the errors.
For true proportions, use a globe, or compare countries with an online true-size tool.
The key idea: A continent is a large landmass, but where one ends is partly human convention, so the count ranges from seven to four.
Part two. Antarctica: the continent of extremes.
The coldest, windiest, highest and driest continent holds most of the world's ice, and lakes hidden kilometres beneath it.
A continent buried in ice.
Antarctica covers about 14 million square kilometres, nearly twice the area of Australia.
Almost all of it lies under an ice sheet averaging around two kilometres thick, and more than four kilometres deep in places.
That ice holds roughly 90 per cent of all the ice on Earth and about 70 per cent of its fresh water.
If it all melted, which would take many thousands of years, global sea levels would rise by close to 60 metres.
The ice is so heavy it presses the land beneath it downward, yet the ice sheet's thickness gives Antarctica the highest average elevation of any continent.
Beneath it lie mountain ranges, valleys and even volcanoes.
Coldest and driest.
On 21 July 1983, at Russia's Vostok Station on the high East Antarctic plateau, thermometers recorded -89.
2 degrees Celsius, the coldest air temperature ever measured directly.
Satellites have since detected snow surfaces below -90 degrees.

Antarctica is colder than the Arctic because it is a high landmass rather than a frozen ocean, its white surface reflects most sunlight, and for months each winter the Sun does not rise over much of it.
Cold air holds little moisture, so the interior receives only a few centimetres of water equivalent a year.
It counts as a desert.
The ice built up because almost nothing melts.
The McMurdo Dry Valleys, largely free of ice and snow, are used to test equipment and ideas for exploring Mars.
Home of the blizzard.
Antarctica's interior is a vast dome of ice, and the air above it becomes intensely cold and dense.
Gravity pulls this heavy air downhill towards the coast, where it can accelerate into ferocious katabatic winds, from a Greek word meaning going down.
Some coastal places are battered almost constantly.
The Australian geologist Douglas Mawson found this out during his Australasian Antarctic Expedition of 1911 to 1914.
His base at Cape Denison in Commonwealth Bay was so wind-lashed that he titled his account The Home of the Blizzard.
Expedition members learned to walk bent almost horizontally into the gusts.
The same expedition saw Mawson's harrowing solo trek back to base after both his companions died.
A continent for science.
Seven countries, including Australia, claim parts of Antarctica.
Australia's claim, the Australian Antarctic Territory, is the largest at about 42 per cent of the continent.
Yet these claims are effectively frozen.
In 1959, at the height of the Cold War, twelve nations signed the Antarctic Treaty, which came into force in 1961.
It bans military activity and nuclear explosions, guarantees freedom of scientific research and requires countries to share their findings.
The Madrid Protocol of 1991 later banned mining and set strict environmental rules.
More than fifty countries have now joined.
Australia runs three permanent research stations on the continent, Casey, Davis and Mawson, and a fourth on sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island.
Hidden lakes, hardy life.
Liquid water lies far beneath the ice.
Radar surveys have found hundreds of subglacial lakes, kept from freezing by the insulating ice above and by heat rising from the Earth below.
The largest known, Lake Vostok, lies under about four kilometres of ice, which Russian drillers reached in 2012.
Some lakes are linked by rivers flowing under the ice sheet.
On the surface, life clings mostly to the coasts.
Penguins, seals and seabirds feed in the rich surrounding ocean, and emperor penguins breed through the dark winter on the sea ice.
There are no native land mammals.
The largest animal living permanently on land is a wingless midge only a few millimetres long.
The key idea: Antarctica is almost twice the size of Australia and holds about 90 per cent of the world's ice.
Part three. Rivers and mountains.
The world's highest peak has seashells at its summit, and nobody can quite agree which river is the longest.
Welcome to the restless shape of the land.
Which river is longest.
Most reference books list the Nile as the longest river, at about 6,650 kilometres.
The Amazon is usually given as about 6,400, but some researchers, including Brazilian scientists in 2007, argue it is longer, up to about 7,000 kilometres.
The question is genuinely unsettled.
Every measurement involves a judgement.
Which headwater stream is the true source: the longest, the biggest or the traditional one?
Where does a wide estuary end?
Rivers also meander, so a more detailed map traces more bends and a longer river.
Published lengths can differ by hundreds of kilometres.
The Yangtze, about 6,300, usually ranks third.
On volume there is no contest: the Amazon carries about a fifth of all the fresh water that rivers deliver to the oceans.
The Murray–Darling.
The Murray River, about 2,500 kilometres long, is Australia's longest.
It rises in the Australian Alps, forms much of the border between New South Wales and Victoria, and reaches the sea in South Australia.
With the Darling, Murrumbidgee and other tributaries, it drains the Murray–Darling Basin: about a million square kilometres across four states and the ACT, roughly one-seventh of Australia.
The basin is the heart of the nation's irrigated farming.
It is also fragile.
Australian rivers are highly variable, and heavy water use plus drought left the Murray mouth needing regular dredging from the early 2000s.
The 2012 Basin Plan aims to share water between farms, towns and the environment.
How mountains rise.
Plate tectonics builds most mountains.
When two continents collide, neither sinks easily, so the crust crumples into fold mountains like the Himalayas and the Alps.
Where an ocean plate dives beneath a continent, melting rock feeds volcanic chains such as the Andes.
Other mountains are single volcanoes, like Kilimanjaro, or blocks of crust lifted along faults.
Meanwhile rain, ice, wind and gravity wear rock down, so young ranges are tall and jagged and old ones low and rounded.
Mount Everest is Earth's highest point above sea level, measured in 2020 at 8,848.
86 metres.
The Himalayas began rising about 50 million years ago when India hit Asia, and still rise a few millimetres a year.
Limestone near the summit holds fossils of sea creatures from an ancient ocean floor.
Highest depends on how.
Everest, on the border of Nepal and China, is known as Sagarmatha in Nepal and Chomolungma in Tibet.
Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa mountaineer, made the first confirmed ascent on 29 May 1953.
But there are other ways to rank mountains.
Mauna Kea in Hawai'i rises only about 4,200 metres above the sea, yet measured from its base on the ocean floor it stands over 10,000 metres, taller than Everest.
Earth bulges at the equator, so the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador, about 6,260 metres high, is the surface point farthest from Earth's centre, roughly 2 kilometres farther out than Everest's peak.
K2, at about 8,600 metres, is the second highest and widely regarded as a much deadlier climb.
Australia's highlands.
Mount Kosciuszko in New South Wales, at 2,228 metres, is the highest mainland peak.
It is modest by world standards, because Australia is old and tectonically quiet and its mountains have eroded for hundreds of millions of years.
In summer it is an easy walk from the Thredbo chairlift.
The Polish explorer Paweł Strzelecki climbed there in 1840 and named it after Tadeusz Kościuszko.
Mawson Peak, an active volcano on remote Heard Island, an Australian external territory, is higher at about 2,745 metres.
The Great Dividing Range, a chain of ranges and plateaus over 3,500 kilometres long from Cape York to the Grampians, shapes the east.
Short, fast rivers drain to the Pacific, while inland rivers flow west towards the Murray–Darling or Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre.
It also casts a rain shadow over the dry interior.
The key idea: The Nile is usually listed as longest at about 6,650 kilometres, but the answer depends on where you say a river starts and ends.
Part four. Everest: the roof of the world.
The highest mountain on Earth is still rising, and its summit is made of rock that formed at the bottom of an ancient sea.
How high is high.
Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and the Tibet region of China.
Measuring it has always been tricky, partly because its snow cap changes depth, and partly because the two countries used different methods and quoted slightly different figures for decades.
In December 2020 they jointly announced a new official height of 8,848.
86 metres, based on satellite positioning and surveyors carrying equipment to the summit.
At that height the air pressure is only about a third of that at sea level, so each breath delivers far less oxygen.
Above about 8,000 metres lies what climbers call the death zone, where the body slowly deteriorates and cannot acclimatise.
Seashells on the summit.
The top of Everest is limestone that formed hundreds of millions of years ago on the floor of a shallow sea.
Geologists have found fossils of marine creatures such as trilobites and crinoids, sea lilies, in it.
How did a seabed end up nearly nine kilometres in the sky?
The answer is plate tectonics.
India was once a separate landmass drifting north across the Tethys Ocean.
When it collided with Asia, sediments from the ocean floor were crumpled, stacked and pushed upwards.
The Himalaya are the result of that crash, which began around 50 million years ago, though geologists debate the exact timing.
India still pushes north by a few centimetres every year.
A mountain still growing.
The collision has not stopped.
Precise satellite measurements show parts of the Himalaya rising by a few millimetres each year.
At the same time, ice, landslides, rivers and frost shatter the rock and carry it away, so the height we see is a constant tug of war between uplift and erosion.
Earthquakes are part of the same process.
The devastating Nepal earthquake of April 2015 was caused by the Indian plate sliding beneath Asia.
It also shifted the land around Everest slightly, one reason the mountain was measured again a few years later.
Names and first ascent.
The mountain has local names: Chomolungma in Tibetan, often translated as goddess mother of the world, and Sagarmatha in Nepali.
British surveyors called it Peak XV until calculations around 1852, in which Radhanath Sikdar is often credited with a key role, showed it to be the highest on Earth.
Surveyor General Andrew Waugh proposed naming it after his predecessor, Sir George Everest, who reportedly objected that locals could not easily write or say it.
The name was adopted in 1865 anyway.
In 1924 George Mallory and Andrew Irvine vanished near the top, and whether they summited is unknown.
On 29 May 1953, Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay stood on the summit.
Hundreds have died trying since.
Highest, but not tallest.
Everest's summit is the highest point above sea level, but there are other ways to measure a mountain.
Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises about 4,200 metres above the sea, yet most of the volcano is underwater.
Measured from its base on the ocean floor, it stands around 10,000 metres, taller than Everest.
Then there is Chimborazo, a volcano in Ecuador only about 6,260 metres above sea level.
Because the Earth spins, it bulges slightly at the equator, and Chimborazo sits near the top of that bulge.
Its summit is therefore the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre, roughly two kilometres farther out than Everest's.
Which mountain is biggest depends on the question you ask.
The key idea: Everest's official height is 8,848.86 metres, agreed by Nepal and China in 2020, and the air there holds about a third of the oxygen at sea level.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do different countries teach different numbers of continents?
Answer. Continents are partly a matter of convention.
Question two. Why does Antarctica's ice sheet matter so much to the planet?
Answer. It holds most of Earth's ice and fresh water.
Question three. Why is it disputed whether the Nile or the Amazon is longer?
Answer. It depends where you place the source and mouth.
Question four. Why does each breath deliver so little oxygen near Everest's summit?
Answer. Air pressure there is about a third of sea level.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
